title: Brand first or site first
metaTitle: Brand first or the site first
excerpt: If the name, the offer, and the sentence are still moving, the site will be rebuilt. A small identity is enough. A long brand program can wait.
alt: Pale blue and orange ink swirls on a white ground, a small mark with a stable color.

faqs.question: What has to be stable before a website is designed?
faqs.answer: The name, the offer, and the sentence under the logo. If those change every week, the site will be redesigned as soon as they settle. A typeface will not discover the offer for you.

faqs.question: How much brand identity does an early site need?
faqs.answer: A wordmark, a type pair, one or two colors, and a rule for pictures are enough. Write them on one page. A long brand program is useful later, when several people publish and the work starts to disagree.

faqs.question: When should you pause the site and settle the name first?
faqs.answer: Pause if you refuse to say the current name to a customer, or if the page would contradict the sales call. Also pause before you print or sign something physical with a mark you expect to replace. Do not pause only because a competitor's site looks more decorated.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
Brand before website is the right order only when the name, the offer, and the sentence are still moving. If those three are unstable, the site you build will be redesigned as soon as they settle. If they are stable, a small identity is enough to design the site. A six-month brand program is not a prerequisite for a page that tells the truth.

Founders delay the site waiting for a brand, and they delay the brand waiting for a perfect name. Meanwhile the only public sentence is a social bio that already disagrees with the product. Stabilize the three things that make a page true. Then ship the page.

## Three things that have to hold

The name. You can say it on a call without flinching, and you can own a domain you are willing to print. It does not need a mythic story. It needs to be the word you will still use when the site is linked from someone else's newsletter.

The offer. One sentence a customer can repeat: who it is for, and what they get. If you have three offers and they do not share a buyer, you have three sites waiting to happen. Pick the one this site is for. The others can be a line, or a later page, not a second homepage inside the first.

The sentence. The offer in the words you will actually put under the logo. Not a tagline workshop. A plain line. "We do X for Y." If you cannot write it, the brand program will not find it by picking a typeface. The typeface will decorate the absence.

When those three hold for a month of real conversations, you can design. When they change every week, stop the visual work. Changing the name after the site is built is a redirect project and a reprint of every file. Changing the offer after the site is built is a rewrite of every section that was doing its job. Do the cheap version of those changes on a document, before anyone opens a component.

[Google's title-link guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) says a page title should describe that page, and that boilerplate titles are a poor way to be understood. If the offer is still moving, every title is provisional. You will ship "Home" and "Product" because the true title would be a lie by Friday. Settle the sentence, then write the titles. The titles are not a later SEO task. They are the offer, repeated where a stranger decides whether to open the link.

## A small identity is enough

A small identity is a name, a way of setting type, one or two colors, and a few rules for pictures. It is enough to make a site feel like one company. It is not a guidelines PDF with forty pages of don'ts.

Type: a pair you can use on the web, with a clear size for the headline and the body. You can choose them in an afternoon and test them on a phone. If they fail at a small size, they fail. The brand is not the specimen poster.

Color: a background, a text color, and one accent you will actually repeat. More colors can come when a chart or a product state needs them. A palette of twelve swatches before you have a page is a delay.

The mark: a wordmark is enough for most early companies. A symbol is worth designing when you need it at tiny sizes, in an app icon or a favicon, and the word will not fit. Illustrator is the right tool for that mark. It does not need a narrative about the hidden meaning of the letterform in order to be used this month.

Pictures: a rule, not a library. "We photograph the work in daylight" or "we use the product, not stock handshakes." Thomas Bewick, a public Hanabi project, is an editorial site for a heritage craft brand. The identity and the site are the same idea: the material is the pictures and the type. A startup with no archive yet can still write the rule and hold to it for the first six photographs.

Write the rules on one page. If the page becomes a book, you have started the six-month program by accident.

## What the site can decide

The site is allowed to finish the identity. Real type in the browser, real line lengths, a navigation that forces you to name the offer: these teach you things a brand workshop will not. Framer or Figma can hold the trial. The production site, when you build it, should use the same decisions. Hanabi builds that production in Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind when the page should be code.

Let the site set the voice by contact with the offer. A brand document that invents a voice in the abstract will be ignored by the person writing the homepage under a deadline. Better to write the homepage first, keep the sentences that sound like you, and call that the voice. The document can record it afterward.

Let the site set hierarchy. What is a headline, what is a label, what is a quiet note. Those roles are the identity as much as the color. A brand program that never sees a form, a price, or an error message is not ready for a product company. The site, or the product, will invent those roles anyway. Be in the room.

Do not let the site set the name or the offer. Those are inputs. If the homepage draft cannot say the offer without a new metaphor every section, go back to the sentence. Do not ask the layout to solve a company that has not chosen.

## When to stop and do the name first

Stop if the name is a placeholder you refuse to say to a customer. Building a site on a placeholder means every share of the link is a small apology. You will rebuild the moment the real name arrives, and you will have trained the early audience on the wrong word.

Stop if the offer on the page would contradict the offer in the sales call. The site will create a second company. People will arrive expecting the page and hear the call, or the reverse. Fix the offer in a document. Then design.

Stop if you are about to print, package, or sign a lease with the mark. Physical things are harder to retract than a homepage. A small, stable mark is worth a pause. A hypothetical rebrand is not.

Do not stop because a competitor's site feels more "finished." Finished often means they have more sections, not a clearer offer. Your one page with a true sentence is further along than their template with a vague one.

Do not stop for a naming committee that meets monthly. Give the decision a date. If the date passes and the name is the one you already use in conversation, that is the name. Ship it.

## The long program you do not need yet

A long brand program studies the category, the audience, and the language, and it produces a system for people you have not hired. Parts of that are valuable later, when several people publish and the work starts to disagree. At the start, the program becomes a place to hide from shipping.

You do not need a workshop to permit yourself a serif. You do not need a 60-page narrative of the brand's personality. You do not need to delay the site until every application, from a trade show booth to a vehicle wrap, has been drawn. You need the name, the offer, the sentence, and enough visual consistency that the page looks intentional.

When the company grows, record what you already do. The type you shipped, the colors in the product, the words you kept. That record is the start of a real system, because it describes behavior. A system drawn before behavior is fan fiction about a company that does not exist yet.

Wabisabi, another public Hanabi site, is a calm brand site. The calm is a decision about the offer, held in the page. It is not evidence that a long program must precede any URL. The page is where the decision becomes visible to a stranger.

If you are unsure whether the sentence is stable, write it at the top of a document and use it for two weeks in real emails. If you are still using it without a wink, design the site. If you rewrote it six times, the site is early. The identity work you need is the sentence, not a new color.

## A practical order

1. Name, offer, sentence. Stay here until a customer has heard them without you translating.
2. A one-page identity: type, color, wordmark, picture rule.
3. The site structure: the pages this offer needs, and the one action.
4. Design those pages and build them.
5. A longer system only when a second designer, a second product, or a second channel starts to drift.

Skip to step 3 if step 2 is blocking you and the sentence is stable. A site in black and white with the right words is a brand. You can add color when the structure is true. You cannot add truth by adding color to a sentence you do not believe.

The next trap, once the sentence exists, is to spend a season researching the audience in order to avoid drawing the page. Sometimes you do need to talk to users. Sometimes you already know the job and you need a prototype. That distinction is the next piece: [research or a faster prototype](/blog/research-or-a-faster-prototype).

If you want to sort the sentence from the site with a studio that does both identity and build, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min).
